title: LIKING GAP
caption:
That conversation you keep replaying in your head? 🔁

Researchers paired strangers for a 5-minute chat. Afterwards, both rated how much they liked the other person, and how much they thought the other person liked them.

On average, people were liked more than they thought. Researchers call it the liking gap.

Why? We're so busy judging ourselves that we miss the signs the other person is enjoying it.

Among new college roommates, the gap lasted for months.

So next time you replay it: they probably liked you more than you think.

Not just you. 💜

Source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018), Psychological Science 29(11)

Send this to the friend who overthinks every conversation.

#notjustyou #likinggap #overthinking #socialanxiety #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: THE BEAUTIFUL MESS
caption:
Still cringing about the thing you admitted? 🫣

In seven studies, people pictured moments of vulnerability: admitting a mistake, confessing their love, improvising a song in front of a jury.

When it was them, it looked more like weakness.
When it was someone else, it looked more like courage.

Researchers call it the beautiful mess effect. Up close, you see every messy detail. From the outside, people see the whole picture.

And follow-up studies found: people who are kinder to themselves show a smaller gap.

So that moment you're cringing about? To them, it might have looked brave. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Bruk, Scholl & Bless (2018), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology · Bruk, Scholl & Bless (2022), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

Send this to someone who just did something brave.

#notjustyou #beautifulmess #vulnerability #selfcompassion #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: THE END OF HISTORY
caption:
Who were you ten years ago? 🕰️

Different person, right? Now think ten years ahead. You'll stay pretty much the same… right?

Researchers asked over 19,000 people aged 18 to 68. At every age, people said they had changed a lot in the past decade, and predicted they would change very little in the next.

Psychologists call it the end of history illusion.

People would pay about $80 to see their favorite band from ten years ago. But about $129 to see today's favorite, ten years from now.

"At every age we think we're having the last laugh, and at every age we're wrong." – Daniel Gilbert

So the person you are right now? Not the final version. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Quoidbach, Gilbert & Wilson (2013), Science · via The New York Times

Tell me: what changed most about you in the last ten years?

#notjustyou #endofhistoryillusion #personalgrowth #psychology #psychologyfacts #science #selfdevelopment

title: FUTURE YOU
caption:
Your brain thinks future you is a stranger. 🧠

In a brain scan study, people thought about themselves now, themselves in ten years, and another person. Thinking about future you looked a lot like thinking about someone else.

And the bigger that gap, the worse people were at saving.

So researchers let people meet their future self: an aged version of their own face, in virtual reality. Afterwards, they put about twice as much into a pretend retirement account.

Next time it's now versus later, picture future you. Not a stranger. You. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Ersner-Hershfield, Wimmer & Knutson (2009), Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience · Hershfield et al. (2011), Journal of Marketing Research

Save this for your next "I'll deal with it later" moment.

#notjustyou #futureself #psychology #money #saving #psychologyfacts #science

title: THE SPOTLIGHT
caption:
Spilled coffee on your shirt and felt like everyone was staring? ☕

Researchers made students wear an embarrassing T-shirt with a giant picture of Barry Manilow into a room full of people.

Afterwards, the students guessed about half the room had noticed. The real number? About a quarter.

Psychologists call it the spotlight effect. You're the center of your own world. But everyone else is busy being the center of theirs.

So that coffee stain? Most people never even saw it. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

Send this to someone who's still thinking about that one moment.

#notjustyou #spotlighteffect #socialanxiety #overthinking #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: SAY IT
caption:
You thought something nice about someone. And didn't say it. 🤐

Maybe it felt awkward. Or not good enough.

Researchers had people write compliments to someone close, then predict how that person would feel. They underestimated how good it felt. And overestimated how awkward it was.

The wording barely mattered. The warmth did.

So say it. It lands better than you think. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Zhao & Epley (2021), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

Who's getting your compliment today? Tag them.

#notjustyou #compliments #kindness #relationships #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: FRESH START
caption:
Why does everything start on a Monday? 📅

Google searches for "diet" spike at the start of every week, every month and every year. Students hit the gym more at the start of a week, a new semester, and right after their birthday.

It's called the fresh start effect. A new date feels like a new chapter. Old slip-ups feel like they belong to the last one.

And it works on demand: calling March 20 "the first day of spring" instead of "the third Thursday in March" made people more likely to start (26% vs. 7% signed up for goal reminders).

So missed Monday? Find another first day. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Dai, Milkman & Riis (2014), Management Science · Dai, Milkman & Riis (2015), Psychological Science

What's your next "first day"? Comment it.

#notjustyou #freshstart #motivation #habits #goals #psychology #science

title: THE GOOD ENDING
caption:
People chose more pain over less. Voluntarily. 🧊

In a classic experiment, people held one hand in painfully cold water (14 °C) for 60 seconds. The other hand got the same 60 seconds, plus 30 more while the water got slightly warmer.

Which one would they repeat? Most chose the longer one (22 of 32).

Memory doesn't add up the minutes. It keeps the worst moment and the ending. Psychologists call it the peak-end rule.

So want a good memory? Give it a good ending. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier (1993), Psychological Science

What's the best ending you remember? Tell me.

#notjustyou #peakendrule #kahneman #memory #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: LOOK UP
caption:
You filmed the whole concert. Now try to remember it. 📱

In a museum study, students looked at some objects and photographed others. The next day, they remembered the photographed ones worse.

Psychologists call it the photo-taking impairment effect. One idea: your brain hands the job to the camera. It's saved, so why remember?

But here's the twist: zooming in on one detail helped people remember the whole object.

So take the photo. Then look up, and actually look. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Henkel (2014), Psychological Science

Save this for your next concert.

#notjustyou #memory #photography #mindfulness #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: NEXT IN LINE
caption:
Round of introductions. Your turn is next. What did the person before you just say? 🤔

No idea, right?

In a classic experiment, people took turns reading words aloud. Afterwards, they barely remembered the words read just before their own turn.

It's called the next-in-line effect. While you rehearse your line, your brain stops recording.

Knowing about it helps: people told to focus on the speaker before them avoided the gap.

So next round: listen first. Then talk. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Brenner (1973), Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior · Bond (1985)

Tag the colleague who always goes right after you.

#notjustyou #nextinlineeffect #memory #socialanxiety #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: BAKER / BAKER
caption:
You remember their face. Their job. Their dog. But not their name. 🙃

In one experiment, people saw a face and were told: "this man is a baker." Others were told: "his name is Baker."

Same word. But the job was remembered far better than the name.

It's called the Baker/baker paradox. A baker comes with bread, flour and ovens. A name like Baker comes with nothing to hold on to.

So give names a hook. Picture Mr. Baker holding a loaf of bread. 🍞

Not just you.

Sources: McWeeny, Young, Hay & Ellis (1987), British Journal of Psychology · Cohen (1990), British Journal of Psychology

What's the trick you use to remember names?

#notjustyou #memory #names #bakerbakerparadox #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: NO TICKLE
caption:
Try to tickle yourself. Nothing, right? 🪶

Your brain predicts the touch before it happens. And what's predicted feels weaker.

Researchers built a robot that stroked people's palm, controlled by their own other hand. When the robot added a tiny delay, just a fraction of a second, it started to tickle.

Your brain cancels out its own surprises. That's why you can't tickle yourself. And why someone else's touch always feels stronger.

Not just you. 🧡

Source: Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert (1999), Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience

Did you just try it? Be honest.

#notjustyou #tickle #brain #neuroscience #psychology #sciencefacts #science

title: PHANTOM BUZZ
caption:
Your phone just buzzed. It didn't. 📳

In one survey, almost nine out of ten students had felt a phantom vibration. For most, it happens every now and then. And most don't find it bothersome.

Your brain is on alert for one signal. So it reads a twitch, or your shirt, as a buzz.

Researchers call it a tactile hallucination. And it's incredibly common.

Your brain isn't broken. It's just listening too hard. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Drouin, Kaiser & Miller (2012), Computers in Human Behavior · Rothberg et al. (2010), BMJ

How many times did you check your phone while watching this?

#notjustyou #phantomvibration #smartphone #brain #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: BRAIN FREEZE
caption:
One spoon of ice cream. And your forehead explodes. 🍦

In a study published in the BMJ, students ate ice cream either fast, or slowly. Eating fast? About 27% got a brain freeze. Slowly? About 12%.

The cold hits the roof of your mouth. But the pain shows up in your forehead. That's called referred pain.

The fix: press your tongue against the roof of your mouth to warm it up.

So your brain isn't freezing. The pain just went to the wrong address. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Kaczorowski & Kaczorowski (2002), BMJ

Team fast or team slow?

#notjustyou #brainfreeze #icecream #body #science #sciencefacts #psychology

title: FIRST NIGHT
caption:
First night in a hotel. And you sleep terribly. 🛏️

Researchers measured people's brains during their first night in a new place. One half of the brain, the left, stayed more alert than the other.

It reacted more to strange sounds. And woke people up faster. By the second night, the difference was gone.

It's called the first-night effect. A built-in night watch. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Tamaki, Bang, Watanabe & Sasaki (2016), Current Biology

Send this to your travel buddy who never sleeps on night one.

#notjustyou #sleep #firstnighteffect #travel #brain #psychology #science

title: SLEEP ON IT
caption:
Stuck on a problem? Go to bed. 😴

In one experiment, people practised a number puzzle that had a hidden shortcut. After a night of sleep, more than twice as many found the shortcut as people who stayed awake.

But only if they had worked on the puzzle first.

So sleeping on it isn't giving up. It's part of the work. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Wagner, Gais, Haider, Verleger & Born (2004), Nature

What's the best idea you ever woke up with?

#notjustyou #sleep #creativity #insight #brain #psychology #science

title: BAD NIGHT
caption:
Bad night? You might push people away. Literally. 😵‍💫

In one study, after a sleepless night, people stopped approaching strangers sooner. They kept others about 18 to 60% farther away.

And over a thousand online viewers, who didn't know, rated them as lonelier. Even worse: watching them made the viewers feel a little lonelier themselves.

So before you decide nobody likes you, maybe just sleep. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Ben Simon & Walker (2018), Nature Communications

Tag someone who needs to hear this tonight.

#notjustyou #sleep #loneliness #mentalhealth #brain #psychology #science

title: SLOW MOTION
caption:
In a crash, time slows down. Right? ⏱️

Researchers dropped volunteers about 30 meters into a net. Free fall. Afterwards, they guessed their own fall had lasted about a third longer than other people's.

But during the fall, they watched a display flashing numbers too fast to read. If time really slowed, they could read them. They couldn't.

Fear makes memory record more detail. And more memory feels like more time. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman (2007), PLoS ONE

Have you ever had a "slow-motion" moment?

#notjustyou #time #fear #memory #brain #psychology #science

title: TWO DAYS
caption:
"This will take two days." Famous last words. 🗓️

Students guessed how long their thesis would take. On average: about 34 days. Even their worst-case guess was 49 days. The real average: 55. Only about three in ten finished on time.

It's called the planning fallacy. We picture the plan. Not the interruptions.

The fix: check how long it took last time. Not how long it should take. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross (1994), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

What's the "two-day task" that took you two weeks?

#notjustyou #planningfallacy #productivity #deadlines #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: THE HOUR BEFORE
caption:
Meeting in an hour? Then you can't really start anything. ⏳

Researchers gave people the same free time. Some of them had an appointment coming up. Those people felt they had about ten minutes less. And in the lab, students reminded of an upcoming task got less done.

Time before a deadline feels shorter than it is.

So batch your meetings. And count the real minutes. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Tonietto, Malkoc & Nowlis (2019), Journal of Consumer Research

Save this for your next calendar cleanup.

#notjustyou #productivity #time #meetings #worklife #psychology #science

title: TAP TO PAY
caption:
Why does paying by card feel like nothing? 💳

In one experiment, people bid on tickets to a sold-out basketball game. Some had to pay cash. Others, by card. The card group was willing to pay more than twice as much.

Researchers call it the pain of paying. Cash hurts. Cards numb it.

Want to spend less? Make it hurt a little. Pay cash, or check your balance first. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Prelec & Simester (2001), Marketing Letters

Cash or card: what's your weakness?

#notjustyou #money #spending #painofpaying #behavioraleconomics #psychology #science

title: BREAK THE FIFTY
caption:
You break a fifty. And somehow it's gone by Friday. 💸

In one experiment, people got five dollars. Either as one bill, or as five ones or coins. Those with small change spent more. The single bill mostly stayed in the pocket.

It's called the denomination effect. A big bill feels too whole to break.

So want to save? Keep it in one piece. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Raghubir & Srivastava (2009), Journal of Consumer Research

Are you a "break it immediately" person?

#notjustyou #money #saving #denominationeffect #behavioraleconomics #psychology #science

title: THE WAITING
caption:
Waiting for a new phone feels like impatience. Waiting for a trip feels like happiness. ✈️

Researchers pinged over 2,000 people at random moments and asked what they were thinking about. People looking forward to an experience were happier than people looking forward to a thing.

Even news reports agreed: people in line for experiences were in better moods than people in line for stuff.

So book the trip early. The waiting is part of the gift. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Kumar, Killingsworth & Gilovich (2014), Psychological Science

What are you looking forward to right now?

#notjustyou #happiness #travel #experiences #money #psychology #science

title: EARWORMS
caption:
That song stuck in your head? It's not random. 🎶

Researchers asked 3,000 people for their most frequent earworms and compared them to equally popular songs. Earworms tend to be faster, with a familiar melodic shape, and one surprising jump or repeat.

The most named earworm: "Bad Romance" by Lady Gaga.

To get rid of one: listen to it all the way through. Or chew gum. In one study, it helped. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Jakubowski, Finkel, Stewart & Müllensiefen (2017), Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts · Beaman et al. (2015), Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology

Which song is stuck in your head right now?

#notjustyou #earworm #music #musicpsychology #brain #psychology #science

title: CHILLS
caption:
Goosebumps from a song? Your brain is doing something wild. 🎧

Researchers scanned people while they listened to music that gave them chills. At the peak, their brains released dopamine, the same reward chemical as food.

But here's the twist: dopamine also flowed before the peak. Just from waiting for it.

So that build-up before the drop? Your brain is paying you to wait. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Salimpoor, Benovoy, Larcher, Dagher & Zatorre (2011), Nature Neuroscience

Which song gives you chills every single time?

#notjustyou #music #chills #dopamine #musicproduction #brain #science

title: SAD SONGS
caption:
Why does sad music feel so good? 🌧️

In a survey of over 700 people, researchers asked how sad music makes them feel. The most common answer wasn't sadness. It was nostalgia. Then peacefulness, and tenderness.

And people reached for it most when they felt lonely or down.

So sad songs aren't making it worse. They're keeping you company. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Taruffi & Koelsch (2014), PLOS ONE

Drop your favorite sad song in the comments.

#notjustyou #sadmusic #music #musicpsychology #nostalgia #psychology #science

title: SPOON
caption:
Say the word "spoon". Again. Again. Again. 🥄

Spoon. Spoon. Spoon. Spoon. Spoon. Spoon.

At some point, it stops sounding like a word. It's called semantic satiation, a term coined by a psychologist in 1962.

Repeat a word enough and the link to its meaning gets tired. Like a muscle.

Your brain isn't glitching. It's just tired of spoon. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Jakobovits (1962), McGill University dissertation · Severance & Washburn (1907), American Journal of Psychology

Try it with your own name. Report back.

#notjustyou #semanticsatiation #language #words #brain #psychology #science

title: TIP OF THE TONGUE
caption:
"It's on the tip of my tongue." 👅

In a classic study, people read definitions of rare words. When they got stuck, they often still knew the first letter. Or how many syllables.

So the word is in there. Just not all at once.

And it's universal: of 51 languages surveyed, 45 have a phrase for it. (German: "Es liegt mir auf der Zunge.")

A small hint, like the first sound, often unlocks it. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Brown & McNeill (1966), Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior · Schwartz (1999), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review

What's the word you always forget?

#notjustyou #tipofthetongue #language #memory #words #psychology #science

title: BOUBA / KIKI
caption:
One of these shapes is called Bouba. The other is Kiki. Which is which? 🔵⭐

You probably said the round one is Bouba. So does almost everyone.

Researchers tested speakers of 25 languages and 10 writing systems. Most matched them the same way.

Round sounds, round lips, round shape. Sharp sounds, sharp shape.

So language isn't completely random. Some sounds come with a shape. 🧡

Not just you.

Sources: Ćwiek et al. (2021), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B · Ramachandran & Hubbard (2001) · Köhler (1929)

Did you pick the same? Tell me in the comments.

#notjustyou #boubakiki #language #linguistics #brain #psychology #science

title: SWIPE FATIGUE
caption:
Ten minutes on a dating app, and suddenly nobody looks good? 📱

In three studies, singles swiped through profiles: yes or no. The longer they swiped, the less often they said yes. They also grew less satisfied, and more pessimistic about their own chances.

Researchers call it a rejection mindset.

So if everyone starts looking wrong, it might be the swiping. Not them. Take a break. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Pronk & Denissen (2020), Social Psychological and Personality Science

Send this to the friend who's been swiping since lunch.

#notjustyou #dating #onlinedating #datingapps #relationships #psychology #science

title: ASK ONE MORE
caption:
Want a second date? Ask one more question. ☕

Researchers analysed over 2,000 speed-dating conversations. People who asked more questions got more second dates. Especially follow-up questions, the ones that show you were listening.

The estimate: one extra question per date, across 20 dates, meant one more "yes".

So less pitching yourself. More: "wait, tell me more about that." 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

What's your go-to first-date question?

#notjustyou #dating #firstdate #relationships #conversation #psychology #science

title: YOUR TYPE
caption:
You have a type. Right? 💘

Before a speed-dating event, people listed what they wanted in a partner. Men said looks mattered more to them. Women said earning potential.

But at the actual dates, those things mattered about the same for men and women. What people said they wanted had little to do with who they actually liked.

So maybe your type is just a theory. Go on the date anyway. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Eastwick & Finkel (2008), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

Has someone ever completely broken your "type"?

#notjustyou #dating #relationships #love #attraction #psychology #science

title: JUST THINK
caption:
You'd rather get an electric shock than sit alone with your thoughts. ⚡

Researchers left students alone in an empty room for up to fifteen minutes. No phone. Just their thoughts. Most of them didn't enjoy it.

Then they added a button that gave a mild electric shock, one the students had said they'd pay to avoid.

Two out of three men pressed it. And one in four women. One man pressed it 190 times.

So if you grab your phone the second you're alone, you're not weird. Thinking is hard work. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Wilson et al. (2014), Science

Would you press it? Be honest.

#notjustyou #boredom #mind #psychology #psychologyfacts #science #overthinking

title: YOU LIED TODAY
caption:
You lied today. Probably more than once. 🤥

In a diary study, people wrote down every lie they told for a whole week. College students lied about twice a day. Other adults, about once.

That's one in three conversations for students. One in five for everyone else.

The most common lies were about feelings: "I love it." "I'm fine." "Great idea." And about twice as many lies protected the liar as protected someone else.

So next time you say "I'm fine", at least you're in good company. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: DePaulo, Kashy, Kirkendol, Wyer & Epstein (1996), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

What's the lie you tell most often? (No judgment.)

#notjustyou #lying #honesty #psychology #psychologyfacts #science #relatable

title: MONEY & HAPPINESS
caption:
Money can't buy happiness? Sorry. It can. 💰

For years, the story was: above $75,000 a year, more money stops making you happier.

Then rival researchers teamed up, using an app that asked people how they felt at random moments. For most people, happiness kept rising with income. Way past $75,000. Only the unhappiest group leveled off, at around $100,000.

So money does help. But if you're deeply unhappy, more of it won't fix everything. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers (2023), PNAS

Agree or disagree? Fight me in the comments.

#notjustyou #money #happiness #wellbeing #psychology #psychologyfacts #science

title: FANTASIES
caption:
Your "weird" fantasy? Probably not that weird. 🔒

Researchers asked over 1,500 adults to rate dozens of fantasies. Very few turned out to be rare. Most were shared by lots of people. Themes of power and control, taking it or giving it up, came up especially often.

As the lead researcher put it: "there are a lot more common fantasies than atypical fantasies."

So that thought you'd never say out loud? You're in good company. And a fantasy is a thought, not a plan. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Joyal, Cossette & Lapierre (2015), Journal of Sexual Medicine

#notjustyou #afterdark #psychology #relationships #intimacy #science #psychologyfacts

title: ONCE A WEEK
caption:
More intimacy, happier couple? Only up to a point. ❤️

Researchers looked at surveys from over 30,000 Americans. For people in relationships, well-being rose with how often they were intimate, up to about once a week. After that, more didn't make people any happier. And for singles, there was no link at all.

It doesn't prove cause and effect: happier couples may simply be intimate more often.

So stop counting. Staying connected matters more than the number. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Muise, Schimmack & Impett (2016), Social Psychological and Personality Science

Send this to someone who keeps comparing.

#notjustyou #afterdark #relationships #couples #intimacy #psychology #science

title: THE KISS
caption:
Kissing is human nature. Right? 💋

Anthropologists looked at 168 cultures around the world. Romantic kissing showed up in fewer than half.

Every culture they studied in the Middle East did it. In South America, only 4 out of 33. And among hunter-gatherers, there was little sign of it at all.

So the kiss isn't universal. It's culture. Which makes it a little more special. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Jankowiak, Volsche & Garcia (2015), American Anthropologist

Did you know this? Tell me in the comments.

#notjustyou #afterdark #kissing #culture #anthropology #love #science

title: FAKED IT
caption:
Ever faked it? You're far from the only one. 🎭

Researchers asked almost 300 college students if they'd ever pretended to orgasm. Among those who'd had intercourse, 2 out of 3 women said yes. And men? More than 1 in 4 (28%). Yes, men too.

The top reasons: it just wasn't going to happen, they wanted it to end, or they didn't want to hurt their partner's feelings.

So it's usually about kindness, not deception. But talking beats performing. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Muehlenhard & Shippee (2010), Journal of Sex Research

Would you rather know? Tell us below 👇

#notjustyou #afterdark #psychology #relationships #intimacy #science #psychologyfacts

title: THE EX
caption:
Slept with your ex? It might not set you back. 💔

In two studies, almost 500 people who'd recently broken up reported on their lives, some of them every single day. Trying to get intimate with an ex did not slow down their recovery. Not day to day, and not two months later.

The people most eager were the ones still attached to their ex. But even for them, it didn't bring more distress.

As the lead researcher put it: the "hand-wringing" may not be warranted. So, no shame. Just be honest with yourself about why. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Spielmann, Joel & Impett (2019), Archives of Sexual Behavior

Send this to the friend who needs to hear it 👀

#notjustyou #afterdark #psychology #relationships #breakup #science #psychologyfacts

title: KINK
caption:
Think kink is niche? Not even close. 🔥

A nationally representative survey asked 2,021 American adults what they had ever tried. At least 30% had tried spanking. More than 1 in 5 had tried role play. About 1 in 5, being tied up or tying someone up. And women and men reported these at similar rates.

So what you call "kinky"? For millions of people, it's just Tuesday. The one rule that matters: consent. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Herbenick et al. (2017), PLoS ONE

Surprised by the numbers? 👇

#notjustyou #afterdark #psychology #relationships #intimacy #science #psychologyfacts

title: AFTERPLAY
caption:
The most underrated part of intimacy? What happens after. 🫶

Researchers surveyed over 300 people, then followed 101 couples for three weeks. On average, people spent about 15 minutes on affection afterwards: cuddling, kissing, talking.

The longer that lasted, the more satisfied people were, with their sex life and with their relationship. Three months later, they were still more satisfied. And for parents, the link was even stronger.

So don't rush off. The cuddle counts. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Muise, Giang & Impett (2014), Archives of Sexual Behavior

Tag someone who needs to stay a little longer 😉

#notjustyou #afterdark #psychology #relationships #intimacy #science #psychologyfacts

title: THE BLUES
caption:
Sad after sex? Even when it was good? You're not broken. 🌧️

Researchers in Australia asked women, and later 1,208 men, how they feel right after intimacy. 46% of women had felt sad, tearful or irritable afterwards at least once. Men? 41%. And 1 in 5 men in the past four weeks alone.

It even happened in loving relationships, after sex that felt good.

It has a name: post-sex blues (postcoital dysphoria). So if it hits you, say it out loud. It's not about them. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Sources: Schweitzer et al. (2015), Sexual Medicine · Maczkowiack & Schweitzer (2019), Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy

title: THE GAP
caption:
In bed, there's a gap nobody talks about. 📊

A survey of 52,588 American adults asked how often they usually orgasm during intimacy.
Straight men: 95%
Straight women: 65%
Lesbian women: 86%

So it's not just biology. Women who orgasmed more often got more oral, longer sessions, and asked for what they wanted.

The gap is real. And it can be closed. Start by talking. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Frederick, St. John, Garcia & Lloyd (2018), Archives of Sexual Behavior

title: THE STOPWATCH
caption:
How long does it actually last? Scientists used a stopwatch. ⏱️

About 500 couples in five countries timed themselves at home for four weeks. The median, from start of intercourse to finish: 5.4 minutes. But it varied a lot: some couples were under three and a half minutes, others over ten.

And sex therapists? They rated 3 to 7 minutes as perfectly adequate.

So, shorter than in the movies. And totally normal. The clock was never the point. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Sources: Waldinger et al. (2005), Journal of Sexual Medicine · Corty & Guardiani (2008), Journal of Sexual Medicine

title: THE DISGUST DIAL
caption:
Why isn't sex gross? Think about it. 🪲

90 women watched one of three films: erotica, extreme sports, or a train ride. Then came the gross part: drink from a cup with a bug in it, handle a condom that looked used (all fake, all clean).

The aroused group found the sexual tasks less disgusting, and was more willing to do them.

Arousal turns the disgust dial down. Otherwise, intimacy would be pretty hard to go through with. So if things feel weird afterwards? That's just the dial turning back up. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Borg & de Jong (2012), PLoS ONE

Never thought about it like that? 👇

title: THE AFTERGLOW
caption:
Good sex keeps working for two whole days. ✨

214 newlywed couples kept a diary for two weeks, every single night. After intimacy, satisfaction stayed higher for about 48 hours. That held for men and women, younger and older.

And couples with a stronger afterglow were happier months later. Their satisfaction dropped less over time.

So it's not just one night. It's a two-day glow. Worth keeping warm. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Meltzer et al. (2017), Psychological Science

title: THEY STARTED IT
caption:
You always think they started it. So do they. 🥊

Researchers had pairs of people press on each other's finger, with exactly the force they had just felt. Nobody matched it. Each turn came back about 38% harder.

Why? Your brain dampens your own touch. So your push feels softer than theirs, even when it isn't. And both sides were sure: "I matched it. They pushed harder."

So in your next fight? You're probably hitting harder than you think. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Shergill, Bays, Frith & Wolpert (2003), Science

title: LIE DETECTOR
caption:
You think you can tell when someone is lying. You can't. 🤥

A huge review pooled 206 studies, with 24,483 people judging lies and truths. Their accuracy: 54%. A coin flip gets 50%. Actual lies were caught less than half the time: 47%.

Why? We mostly assume people tell the truth. So most lies slip right through.

Your gut feeling? Basically a coin flip, with confidence. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Bond & DePaulo (2006), Personality and Social Psychology Review

Still think you'd catch them? 👇

#notjustyou #psychology #lying #truth #brain #science #psychologyfacts

title: NOBODY HELPS?
caption:
Get attacked in public, and nobody helps? That's a myth. 🎥

Researchers analyzed security camera footage of 219 real street fights in Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lancaster. In 9 out of 10, at least one stranger stepped in. And the more people were around, the more likely someone helped.

So strangers do show up. Next time, be one of them. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Philpot, Liebst, Levine, Bernasco & Lindegaard (2020), American Psychologist

Faith in humanity: restored? 👇

#notjustyou #psychology #bystandereffect #humanity #socialpsychology #science #psychologyfacts

title: REVENGE
caption:
Revenge feels sweet. Until you actually get it. 🍋

In an experiment, a player secretly cheated his group in a money game. Some players then got the chance to punish him. Everyone who could punish him, did. And they ended up feeling worse than those who couldn't.

Both groups were sure revenge would feel good. It didn't. Punishing kept them thinking about it. The others just moved on.

So revenge doesn't close the wound. It keeps it open. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Carlsmith, Wilson & Gilbert (2008), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

Ever regretted getting even? 👇

#notjustyou #psychology #revenge #emotions #mentalhealth #science #psychologyfacts

title: MIXED SIGNALS
caption:
She smiled. So she's into you? Maybe not. 😶

About 200 students went speed dating, then rated how interested each partner was in them. Men tended to overestimate women's sexual interest. Women tended to underestimate men's.

The worst readers: men looking for something casual, and men who were most attracted to her.

The more you want it, the worse you read it. So ask. Don't guess. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Perilloux, Easton & Buss (2012), Psychological Science

title: NO FEAR
caption:
She was held at knifepoint. And felt no fear. 🔪

She's known only as S.M. A rare disease destroyed a tiny part of her brain on both sides: the amygdala. Researchers took her to a haunted house. She laughed and poked a monster in the head. In a pet store, she kept asking to touch the snakes.

Then they had her breathe air with extra carbon dioxide. And she panicked. A feeling she said was completely new.

Fear of the world outside needs the amygdala. Fear from inside your own body doesn't. So fear isn't one thing. It's at least two. 🧡

Not just you. (Case study: one person, so handle with care.)

Sources: Feinstein, Adolphs, Damasio & Tranel (2011), Current Biology · Feinstein et al. (2013), Nature Neuroscience

Would you want to feel no fear? 👇

title: SAY THE COLOR
caption:
Quick test. Say the COLOR of each word, not the word. Out loud. 🎨

Round one: easy. Round two: not so much. Slower? Did you stumble? Almost everyone does.

Your brain reads automatically. It reads the word before you can stop it, and then it has to fight itself. It's called the Stroop effect, first described in 1935, and it still catches almost everyone.

You can't not read. Try it on a friend. 🧡

Not just you.

Source: Stroop (1935), Journal of Experimental Psychology

How many did you get wrong in round two? 👇

#notjustyou #psychology #brain #braintest #stroopeffect #science #psychologyfacts

title: THE YAWN
caption:
You'll probably yawn before this video ends. 🥱

In one study, over a quarter of people yawned just from reading about yawning. Watching someone yawn works even better: most people caught it within five minutes.

But why do we yawn at all? Science still doesn't know. One idea: it cools your brain. Another: it's about empathy, since people who catch yawns easily may be more tuned in to others. Neither is settled.

So if you yawned just now? Nobody knows exactly why. Comment "Y" if you did. 🧡

Not just you. (Unsolved: these are theories, not answers.)

Source: Provine (1986), Ethology · plus ongoing research on brain cooling and empathy

#notjustyou #psychology #yawning #brain #unsolved #science #psychologyfacts

title: PROFILE LIES
caption:
Your date lied on their profile. 81% do. 📱

Researchers met 80 online daters in person, measured their height and weight, and checked their ID. 81% had fudged at least one: height, weight, or age. Women tended to shave off pounds. Men tended to add inches.

But the lies were small. About five pounds, a third of an inch, a few months. Small enough to get away with. Big enough to feel better.

Be honest. Did you? 👀

Not just you. (Small study: 80 people.)

Source: Toma, Hancock & Ellison (2008), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

#notjustyou #dating #onlinedating #psychology #relationships #science #psychologyfacts

title: THE TALL TAX
caption:
Every inch you're taller is worth money. About $789 a year. 📏

Researchers followed about 8,500 people from their teens into their careers, in the US and the UK. Even after accounting for gender, age and weight, taller people earned more.

6'0" versus 5'5"? That's about $166,000 over a 30-year career. One explanation: height makes people seem more confident, and they get treated that way.

Unfair? Absolutely. But now you know it's there.

Not just you.

Source: Judge & Cable (2004), Journal of Applied Psychology

Tall people: did you know? Short people: are you mad? 👇

#notjustyou #psychology #money #career #bias #science #psychologyfacts

title: YOUR EX IS A DRUG
caption:
Can't stop thinking about your ex? Your brain treats them like a drug. 💔

Researchers scanned people who had just been dumped, but were still madly in love, while they looked at a photo of their ex. The photo lit up the brain's reward and craving system, the same areas involved in cocaine addiction. And regions tied to physical pain lit up too.

The good news: the longer it had been since the breakup, the weaker part of that attachment signal got.

So it's not weakness. It's withdrawal. And withdrawal ends. 🧡

Not just you. (Small study: 15 people.)

Source: Fisher, Brown, Aron, Strong & Mashek (2010), Journal of Neurophysiology

Stub your toe and swear? Good. It actually helps. #@!% 🧊

Students held a hand in ice water as long as they could. Once repeating a swear word, once repeating a neutral word. While swearing, they lasted about 40 seconds longer. And it hurt less. Their heart rate went up, too.

One idea: swearing triggers a small fight-or-flight response, and that dulls the pain.

So next time it hurts? Let it out.

Not just you.

Source: Stephens, Atkins & Kingston (2009), NeuroReport

title: 80 MILLION
caption:
One 10-second kiss. 80 million bacteria. 💋

Researchers studied 21 couples. One partner drank a yogurt drink with traceable bacteria, then they kissed for ten seconds. Afterwards, those bacteria had tripled in the other partner's saliva: about 80 million swapped in one kiss.

Couples who kissed at least nine times a day had noticeably more similar saliva bacteria. Oh, and the men said they kissed ten times a day. The women said five. 🤔

So yes, kissing literally makes you more alike. At least in your mouth.

Not just you · After Dark (Small study: 21 couples.)

Source: Kort et al. (2014), Microbiome

title: WHO CHEATS
caption:
1 in 5 married men has cheated. And women? Closer than you think. 💍

A big national survey asked married Americans one question: have you ever had sex with someone else while married? 20% of men said yes. 13% of women.

But under 30, women were slightly ahead: 11% versus 10%. The highest rate of all? Men in their seventies: 26%.

So the real cheater is older than the stereotype. And most people never do it.

Not just you · After Dark

Source: General Social Survey, analysis by Wang (2018), Institute for Family Studies

Surprised by the age thing? 👇

title: OUT OF YOUR LEAGUE
caption:
You're messaging people out of your league. Everyone is. 💬

Researchers analyzed a big dating site in four US cities and ranked every user by how desirable they were to others. Most people messaged someone about 25% more desirable than themselves.

Most of those messages got no answer. But about 1 in 5 people who aimed up did get a reply. And on that site, men's desirability kept rising until about 50. Women's fell from 18 on.

So aim high. Just don't take the silence personally.

Not just you.

Source: Bruch & Newman (2018), Science Advances

title: THE CHARMER
caption:
The most charming person in the room? Might be a narcissist. 🪞

Students who had never met rated each other after short introductions. The more narcissistic someone was, the more they were liked at first sight. It was all surface: stylish clothes, confident body language, an entertaining way of talking.

But in another study, groups met again and again. By the seventh meeting, the narcissists' ratings had flipped: from likable to disliked.

So first impressions are easy to fake. Give it seven meetings.

Not just you.

Sources: Back, Schmukle & Egloff (2010), JPSP · Paulhus (1998), JPSP

caption:
Who uses sex toys more, men or women? It's closer than you think. 🗄️

Two national surveys asked over 3,000 American adults about vibrators. 53% of women had used one. And men? 45%, most of them together with a partner.

Users were also more likely to look after their sexual health, like doing self-exams (a link, not proof).

So it's not a secret-drawer thing. It's half the country. Both halves.

title: WHO'S KINKIER
caption:
Who's kinkier, men or women? Get ready. 🔗

Researchers asked over a thousand adults about unusual sexual interests. Almost half had at least one, and a third had actually tried one.

Fetishes? Women reported a bit more than men (48% vs 40%). Pain and submission? Women too: 28% versus 19%. Men led in other areas, but the gap was far smaller than the stereotype.

So the kinky one in your relationship might not be who you think. 😏

title: THE SEX RECESSION
caption:
Think we're wilder than our parents? We're having less sex. 📉

A national survey has asked Americans about their sex lives since 1989, over 26,000 people. By the early 2010s, adults had sex about 9 times less per year than in the late 90s. For married couples, the drop was even bigger: 16 times less a year.

One reason researchers point to: fewer young people have a steady partner.

So we might talk about sex more. But we're having less of it.

Source: Twenge, Sherman & Wells (2017), Archives of Sexual Behavior

title: BLIND DAY
caption:
A dating site turned off every photo. For one day. 🙈

On "Love Is Blind Day", OkCupid hid all pictures for seven hours. People answered first messages 44% more often, and conversations went deeper.

Then, at 4 p.m., the photos came back. About 2,200 conversations had started blind. They just melted away.

Without a face, we were kinder. With one, we got picky.

Would you date blind? 👇

title: FAKE MATCH
caption:
What if your perfect match is a lie? 💔

OkCupid took pairs who were a bad match, just 30%, and told them they were 90%. They messaged more. And they acted like a good match, even though they weren't.

The site's own verdict: "the mere myth of compatibility works just as well as the truth."

When OkCupid admitted it in 2014, users were furious.

So maybe chemistry is partly what you're told to expect. 🧪

Not just you · Platform experiment (OkCupid, not peer-reviewed)

title: NOBODY READS IT
caption:
You spent an hour on your dating bio. Nobody read it. ✍️

OkCupid had people rate profiles for looks and personality. Some saw the text, some saw only the photo. The scores barely moved: your text made up less than 10% of what people thought of you.

And looks versus personality? For 92% of profiles, the two scores were almost the same. 😬

So your words matter. Your photo just talks louder.

Not just you · Platform experiment (OkCupid, not peer-reviewed)

Source: Christian Rudder, "We Experiment On Human Beings!", OkCupid blog (2014)

title: THE OLD PHOTO
caption:
That hot profile photo? It's probably old. 📸

OkCupid compared what users claim with what its data shows. People are about two inches shorter than they say. And 20% poorer.

But the best part: over a third of the hottest photos were at least a year old. Hot photos were more than twice as likely to be 3+ years old (12% vs 5%).

So the better the photo, the older it probably is. 👀

Not just you · Platform data (OkCupid, 2010, not peer-reviewed)

OkCupid analyzed how its users rated each other's looks. Women were harsh: 80% of men landed below medium. Men rated women on a fair curve, most women right in the middle.

But men's messages? Two thirds went to the best-looking third of women.

So women judge harder. Men chase harder.

On OkCupid, men of every age rated women in their early 20s highest. Women's taste grew up with them: their ideal age rose with their own.

But here's the twist: men mostly messaged women close to their own age.

One guess: if others aren't into you, I see less competition. Being "just cute" is a curse.
